# ROUTINE BOOK (age 0-1)

The child this book is for is one or younger. Write for that child. These rules override any
instruction elsewhere to build a conflict, a tension or a challenge.

**A day, not a plot.** The book follows the rhythm of an ordinary day: waking, being dressed, eating,
playing, going out, greeting the animals, coming back, winding down, sleep. That order is the whole
structure, and it is enough. The child is on every page.

**A new thing on every page.** The book is a string of small moments, never one situation stretched
across the book: on every page something is seen, met, heard, touched or done that no earlier page
had. Never carry one want from page to page — wanting a thing, still wanting it, then getting it is
three wasted pages.

**Naming and repetition are the payoff.** The pleasure of the book is pointing at a thing and saying
what it is, and hearing the same shape of sentence come round again. Name what is there — the animal,
the food, the coat, the boot — and let a phrase return across the pages.

**The child's traits are the plan, where there are any.** Give each trait a page of its own, shown
the way a child this age shows it — brave is patting something big, strong is dragging something
heavy for them, adventurous is climbing up to look over, clever is naming and matching, cheerful is
laughing and clapping. Whatever the child is said to love appears in the book and gets a page of its
own — one page each, never the whole book. Where no traits are given, use what every small child is:
hungry, sleepy, curious, delighted, grumpy.

**Show three different feelings.** Two at the least, three is better, each plain on the face and in
what the body does: delight, surprise, and a moment of being upset or sad. The last page is happy.

**One small thing goes wrong, and comes right.** Something is taken, dropped, blown away or will not
work; the child minds, and it is put right within a page or two — that is the whole storyline, and
it is enough.

**Nothing frightening.** Never dangerous, nobody unkind on purpose, and never anything the child has
to work out to fix.

**What the child does.** Make-believe doing is the point: standing at the wheel, holding a rope,
waving at a bird, splashing, feeding, patting, pointing, naming, carrying, giving, hiding, falling
over and getting up again. Never anything that turns on working something out — reading, following
clues, making a plan, solving a puzzle, or deciding for others.

**The child does the doing.** A grown-up may be right beside them — carrying them, holding
the thing out, steadying them — and the doing on the page is still the child's: they pat, splash, feed,
point, carry, give. Never a page where a grown-up's hands do the only thing that happens.

**No real-world errands alone.** No stations, tickets, traffic, shops or crowds the child gets
through by themselves. Inside the story's own make-believe world they may sail, ride, fly or be
carried anywhere at all.

**Topic.** A place full of things to look at, a child let loose in it, and one small thing that goes
wrong and comes right. Never a quest, a search, a rescue, a secret or a prize. A costume or a
favourite theme is what the child wears and what the pages are full of, never a mission they carry
out.

**Food.** Only ordinary food a child of this age eats, named plainly. Never sweets or ice cream, and
never anything a small child cannot chew or swallow safely.

**Nothing appears from nowhere.** A thing is referred to as known only after a page has shown it
there. Nothing valuable, exciting or edible is simply found.

**A make-believe story opens and closes where the child really is.** Page one shows them there,
dressing up or beginning to play, and the last page brings them back to that same place. Never move
them to somewhere real they were never shown leaving for.

**A life event is weather, not a task.** What changes around the child, and what stays the same in
their hands. Never something they understand, say, explain or put right.

**Ending.** Home, a meal or sleep. A small thing may go well — a first taste, a first step up, a
thing carried all the way — shown happening and not remarked on. No prize, no ceremony, no line
about what it means or what the child will be from now on.

**The age owns the props and the subject.** What the main character wants, what stands in the way, and the objects the story turns on belong to the world of someone that age — what they handle themselves, where they go on their own, what counts as a loss to them. Never a want, a comfort or a plaything the reader has outgrown, and never stakes beyond what someone that age would be given.

This idea has the shape: a thing that grows — something small in the main character's care gets bigger, and what it needs grows with it. Keep the shape; the shape is a requirement, not a choice.

Generate a story idea that includes:
1. THE SETUP: who is there and what they want.
2. WHAT STANDS IN THE WAY.
3. THE TURN: something that changes what the reader expected.
4. THE PROMISE: one thing that happens in this book.
5. WHAT IT COSTS THEM TO FAIL.

The reader already chose the town and the season. Do not open with an address. The place is the scene the action happens in, named where the action is, never a sentence that states where and when.

The want, the obstacle and the cost are each a concrete thing the reader can name: one thing to reach, fetch, mend or be in time for, a stated force or condition against it, and a stated loss. Wanting to find out what something is, an unnamed something standing in the way, or more than they can see, are none of the three.

Stop there. Never write how it ends, and never write the middle: no naming the object, gate, figure or trick that decides the outcome, no test the characters will have to pass, and no pairing of a character's trait with the obstacle it will meet. Say who they are, not what each of them will do about it.

STORY LENGTH: SHORT (1-10 pages) - 6 sentences max per idea

The page count sets how much story gets written later, never how much of it is given away here. A long book gets the same short back-cover text as a short one.

## WHAT MAKES A PARENT BUY IT

The idea answers these:
- What does the child get to do here that they cannot do at home?
- What in it will they laugh at, or gasp at?
- What is frightening here in the way a child likes being frightened?
- Which sentence makes them ask for this book again tomorrow?

RULES:
- No adjectives allowed. Do not describe things as "magical", "brave", "beautiful", "exciting", etc.
- Four to six sentences, whatever the page count, and at most one sentence per slot. A longer text turns into a plot summary.
- One sentence is the turn: something changes what the reader expected. The thing acts back, the wrong person is believed, the helper turns out to need help. It stands between the obstacle and the event, and it names neither the middle nor the ending.
- One sentence is an event this book contains, written in the story's voice as a thing that happens and can be pictured. It never addresses the reader and never names the reader, the book, the page or the picture. Never whether they manage it, and never what decides it. It stands after the obstacle.
- No sentence runs past about 30 words. A sentence that needs a dash to hold two clauses together is two sentences.
- The last sentence states what failing costs, and the cost is something of theirs. Nothing comes after it.
- [FINAL] holds the idea text only: no notes, no headings, no second version, no commentary.
- Nothing in the story or its pictures is dangerous enough that it could lead to death — for anyone. Frightening is the right level. No child is left alone at a height or on an edge, and no cost ends on a child never coming home. A historical event keeps the danger it really had: tell it at a child's level, never remove it.
- Be specific about locations and time periods.
- The outline should focus on the main characters
- All the characters must be mentioned
- A character is in the idea through what they want, what they are answerable for, or the part of the main character's want they hold: someone waiting for them, someone they fetch it for. That is presence.
- The youngest main character does something in the idea. An adult is in the idea only when the story needs them, and then they want something of their own.
- The want is the main character's own want, stated as theirs, and they are the one who sets out after it. An errand an adult handed them is not their want. For a main character aged two or under the want is something to reach, follow, touch, hold or get to, never an object to fetch back and never an arrangement to sort out.
- One thing in the idea is out of the ordinary and can be pointed at in a picture: a thing, a creature, a place or an event, named with a plain noun. It stands in the first or second sentence and belongs to the setup or to the obstacle, never to what decides the outcome. It is named and never explained: not what it does, not what it opens, not who it obeys, not why it is as it is.
- The want is one a child would have for themselves: something to reach, to keep, to get into, to be first at, to give to someone, or to be allowed. A submission, a measurement, a permit, a set of numbers, or a repair an adult is paid to do is not one.
- Follow the SCENE COMPLEXITY guide above - match story complexity to the number of scenes

EXAMPLES of good story ideas:

Example 1: "A stone in the wall of a ruin sits loose, and behind it is a way into somewhere that is on no map. A child wants the little carved animal their grandmother lost in there when she was small. Whoever keeps that gap says the animal belongs to him now. Then he says the grandmother's name, and he says it as though he has been waiting for her. The child squeezes through the wall with the evening bell already ringing at home. If the last bell goes first, the animal stays his, and the grandmother has only the story of it."

Example 2: "A bone as long as an arm lies half out of the gravel at the foot of a quarry. A child wants to carry it up to their grandfather, who is the only one who will know what animal it came from. An older brother says it is a stick and walks on, and the gate at the top of the path is locked when the sun goes down. The gravel slides, and there is more of the animal under it than one child can carry. The child kneels in the gravel and digs with both hands while the light turns orange. If the gate closes first, the whole of it goes back under, and nobody ever hears what it was."

Example 3: "A goat is standing on the kitchen table eating the birthday cake. A child wants that cake out in the garden, where everyone is already singing. The goat is bigger than the child and will not be pushed. The singing stops, and the whole garden decides it was the child who let the goat in. The child stands in the doorway and holds out an apple in both hands. If the cake never comes out, it stays the child's fault for as long as anyone remembers that birthday."

EVENT: First Powered Flight (December 17, 1903)

HISTORICAL CONTEXT:
Wilbur and Orville Wright were bicycle mechanics from Dayton, Ohio, who became obsessed with
the dream of human flight. They studied birds, built their own wind tunnel, and tested over
200 wing designs. Unlike other inventors who focused on powerful engines, the Wrights realized
the key was controlling the aircraft in flight.

They invented "wing warping" - twisting the wings to turn and balance the plane. They chose
Kitty Hawk, North Carolina for its steady winds and soft sandy landing surface. After years
of glider tests, they added a lightweight gasoline engine they built themselves.

On December 17, 1903, Orville made the first powered flight, lasting 12 seconds and covering
120 feet. They made four flights that day, with the longest lasting 59 seconds and covering
852 feet. The age of aviation had begun, though few newspapers reported it and many didn't

the key was controlling the aircraft in flight.

of glider tests, they added a lightweight gasoline engine they built themselves.

120 feet. They made four flights that day, with the longest lasting 59 seconds and covering
852 feet. The age of aviation had begun, though few newspapers reported it and many didn't
believe it was true for years.

# HERO'S JOURNEY (age 10)

The child this book is for is ten. Write for that child.

**The full shape, at full size.** Ordinary world, then a call that pulls the main character out of it,
then challenges that get harder, then a moment where all seems lost, then the turn, then home —
changed. Every one of those beats is on the page, in that order.

**A real low point is required.** Before the end there is a page where the plan has failed, the thing
is lost, or the friend is gone, and it looks like it will stay that way. Do not soften it into a
small setback and do not skip past it in a line.

**The hero's own idea turns it.** What saves the day comes out of the main character — something they
noticed earlier, a strength of theirs, a thing they were told and remembered. Never luck, never a
grown-up arriving to fix it, never a power handed over at the last moment.

**It resolves.** The turn comes before the last page and they come home changed. Never a story that
stops on the problem.

**A real antagonist is allowed.** Someone who wants something opposed to what the main character
wants, with a reason of their own. A twist, a sidekick who earns their place, and a setup on an early
page that pays off at the end all belong here.

**Competence.** The main character does things: decides, tries, fails, adapts. They are never carried
through their own story.

**The stake is the main character's own.** What is wanted and what is at risk belong to their own
life — never a piece of work set for them, an assignment, a submission, a competition entry, or a
place to be won in a selection. What stands in the way is something they can reach out and touch, or
someone who wants the opposite, never a procedure, a schedule or a system to be satisfied. What is at
risk is a person or a creature they care about, never a promise made to themselves, a recording or a
machine's state. The thing out of the ordinary is one they hold or touch, never one they operate.

**Humour and mild peril.** A chase, a close call, a night out in the cold are fine. Nothing gory,
nothing cruel, nobody the reader likes is really harmed.

**Ending.** They come back to where they started and it reads differently, because they are different.

**The age owns the props and the subject.** What the main character wants, what stands in the way, and the objects the story turns on belong to the world of someone that age — what they handle themselves, where they go on their own, what counts as a loss to them. Never a want, a comfort or a plaything the reader has outgrown, and never stakes beyond what someone that age would be given.

This idea has the shape: a promise to keep — the main character has given their word, and keeping it costs more than they thought. Keep the shape; the shape is a requirement, not a choice.

Generate a story idea that includes:
1. THE SETUP: who is there and what they want.
2. WHAT STANDS IN THE WAY.
3. THE TURN: something that changes what the reader expected.
4. THE PROMISE: one thing that happens in this book.
5. WHAT IT COSTS THEM TO FAIL.

The reader already chose the town and the season. Do not open with an address. The place is the scene the action happens in, named where the action is, never a sentence that states where and when.

The want, the obstacle and the cost are each a concrete thing the reader can name: one thing to reach, fetch, mend or be in time for, a stated force or condition against it, and a stated loss. Wanting to find out what something is, an unnamed something standing in the way, or more than they can see, are none of the three.

Stop there. Never write how it ends, and never write the middle: no naming the object, gate, figure or trick that decides the outcome, no test the characters will have to pass, and no pairing of a character's trait with the obstacle it will meet. Say who they are, not what each of them will do about it.

The idea answers these:
- What does the child get to do here that they cannot do at home?
- What in it will they laugh at, or gasp at?
- What is frightening here in the way a child likes being frightened?
- Which sentence makes them ask for this book again tomorrow?

EXAMPLES of good story ideas:

Example 1: "A stone in the wall of a ruin sits loose, and behind it is a way into somewhere that is on no map. A child wants the little carved animal their grandmother lost in there when she was small. Whoever keeps that gap says the animal belongs to him now. Then he says the grandmother's name, and he says it as though he has been waiting for her. The child squeezes through the wall with the evening bell already ringing at home. If the last bell goes first, the animal stays his, and the grandmother has only the story of it."

Example 2: "A bone as long as an arm lies half out of the gravel at the foot of a quarry. A child wants to carry it up to their grandfather, who is the only one who will know what animal it came from. An older brother says it is a stick and walks on, and the gate at the top of the path is locked when the sun goes down. The gravel slides, and there is more of the animal under it than one child can carry. The child kneels in the gravel and digs with both hands while the light turns orange. If the gate closes first, the whole of it goes back under, and nobody ever hears what it was."

Example 3: "A goat is standing on the kitchen table eating the birthday cake. A child wants that cake out in the garden, where everyone is already singing. The goat is bigger than the child and will not be pushed. The singing stops, and the whole garden decides it was the child who let the goat in. The child stands in the doorway and holds out an apple in both hands. If the cake never comes out, it stays the child's fault for as long as anyone remembers that birthday."

8. Thema: Das Wright-Brüder-Thema ist das Hindernis selbst – der Flyer, der noch nie geflogen ist, der Wind, der dagegen spricht. Die Idee funktioniert nicht ohne das Thema. Korrekt.

9. Hook: Das aussergewöhnliche Ding: «ein hölzernes Gefährt aus Stoff und Drähten» – steht in Satz 1 (Setup). Es wird nicht erklärt, was es tut oder wem es gehorcht. Korrekt.

10. Das Kind handelt: Amir will fliegen und legt sich selbst auf die Maschine (S5). Yara läuft neben dem Flügel – sie handelt aktiv. Der Wille ist Amirs eigener, kein Auftrag eines Erwachsenen. Gewinn für Amir: Beweis. Korrekt.

11. Versprechen: S5 – «Amir legt sich auf die Maschine und Yara läuft neben dem Flügel her, die Hände bereit.» – das ist ein Ereignis, das man sich vorstellen kann, sagt nicht, ob sie es schaffen. Korrekt. Kein Anreden des Lesers. Korrekt.

12. Wende: S4 – «Dann sagt einer der Männer, dass ein anderer Erfinder aus dem Osten bereits auf dem Weg nach Kitty Hawk ist.» Das verändert die Erwartung: nicht nur der Wind ist das Problem, jetzt ist auch die Zeit ein Feind. Es sagt nicht, wie die Geschichte weitergeht. Korrekt, aber der fremde Erfinder braucht mehr Glaubwürdigkeit.

13. Form: «Ein Versprechen zu halten» – Amir hat Yara versprochen, dass es klappt. Das Einhalten kostet mehr als gedacht (Wind + Gegner + Zeitdruck). Die Form ist vorhanden.

14. Eröffnung: S1 – «Am Strand von Kitty Hawk liegt…» – das benennt den Ort, aber sofort mit dem aussergewöhnlichen Ding. Es ist grenzwertig, da es mit Ort und Zeit beginnt. Besser wäre ein direkterer Einstieg mit dem Ding selbst.

15. Länge: 6 Sätze – korrekt. Längster Satz (S2): über 30 Wörter – muss gekürzt werden.

16. Würde ein Elternteil es kaufen?
- Was darf das Kind hier tun, was es zuhause nicht kann? → Auf einer Flugmaschine liegen, als erstes Kind der Welt abzuheben versuchen. Vorhanden (S5).
- Worüber lachen oder staunen? → Der fremde Mann, der anreist, um alles zu verhindern – staunenswert. Aber kein Lachen. Fehlt.
- Was ist erschreckend auf die Art, wie Kinder es mögen? → Der Gegner auf dem Weg – aber zu vage. Schwach.
- Welcher Satz lässt sie morgen wieder nach dem Buch fragen? → S5 ist bildhaft, aber noch nicht stark genug.

Fünf Verbesserungen:

1. Grammatikfehler korrigieren: «seinem kleinen Schwester» → «seiner kleinen Schwester».
2. S2 kürzen: er ist zu lang (über 30 Wörter) und muss in zwei kürzere Sätze aufgeteilt werden.
3. S3 aufteilen: der Satz verbindet zwei Teilsätze mit Komma und «und» in einer Weise, die nahe an einem Gedankenstrich-Verstoss ist – sauberer trennen.
4. Den Kostensatz (S6) konkretisieren: «gehört das Versprechen dem Wind» ist zu poetisch und abstrakt; der Verlust muss benennbar und greifbar sein – zum Beispiel: Yara glaubt Amir nie wieder, wenn er es verspricht.
5. Eine Spur Humor oder Staunen einbauen, das Eltern und Kinder anspricht – der fremde Mann könnte mit einem Detail eingeführt werden, das ihn lebendig macht, ohne die Wende zu verraten.

CUT: nichts zu schneiden nach Regel 6.

[FINAL]

Rollen:
Amir: Orville Wright (Pilot des ersten Fluges)
Yara: Wilbur Wright (läuft neben dem Flugzeug her und hält es im Gleichgewicht)

Ein Gefährt aus Holz, Stoff und Drähten liegt im Sand von Kitty Hawk, und noch kein Mensch hat es je vom Boden weggebracht. Amir hat Yara versprochen: Heute fliegt es. Der Wind am Kill Devil Hills bläst so stark, dass die Männer den Kopf schütteln und sagen, heute sei kein Tag zum Fliegen. Dann taucht am Strand eine Gestalt in einem schwarzen Mantel auf, die sagt, der Flyer gehöre ihr, und die einen Zettel in der Hand hält. Amir legt sich auf die Maschine und Yara läuft neben dem Flügel her, beide Hände ausgestreckt gegen den Wind. Wenn der Flyer nicht aufsteigt, bevor die Gestalt näher kommt, glaubt Yara Amir nie wieder, wenn er ihr etwas verspricht.

# HERO'S JOURNEY (age 10)

The child this book is for is ten. Write for that child.

**The full shape, at full size.** Ordinary world, then a call that pulls the main character out of it,
then challenges that get harder, then a moment where all seems lost, then the turn, then home —
changed. Every one of those beats is on the page, in that order.

**A real low point is required.** Before the end there is a page where the plan has failed, the thing
is lost, or the friend is gone, and it looks like it will stay that way. Do not soften it into a
small setback and do not skip past it in a line.

**The hero's own idea turns it.** What saves the day comes out of the main character — something they
noticed earlier, a strength of theirs, a thing they were told and remembered. Never luck, never a
grown-up arriving to fix it, never a power handed over at the last moment.

**It resolves.** The turn comes before the last page and they come home changed. Never a story that
stops on the problem.

**A real antagonist is allowed.** Someone who wants something opposed to what the main character
wants, with a reason of their own. A twist, a sidekick who earns their place, and a setup on an early
page that pays off at the end all belong here.

**Competence.** The main character does things: decides, tries, fails, adapts. They are never carried
through their own story.

**The stake is the main character's own.** What is wanted and what is at risk belong to their own
life — never a piece of work set for them, an assignment, a submission, a competition entry, or a
place to be won in a selection. What stands in the way is something they can reach out and touch, or
someone who wants the opposite, never a procedure, a schedule or a system to be satisfied. What is at
risk is a person or a creature they care about, never a promise made to themselves, a recording or a
machine's state. The thing out of the ordinary is one they hold or touch, never one they operate.

**Humour and mild peril.** A chase, a close call, a night out in the cold are fine. Nothing gory,
nothing cruel, nobody the reader likes is really harmed.

**Ending.** They come back to where they started and it reads differently, because they are different.

**The age owns the props and the subject.** What the main character wants, what stands in the way, and the objects the story turns on belong to the world of someone that age — what they handle themselves, where they go on their own, what counts as a loss to them. Never a want, a comfort or a plaything the reader has outgrown, and never stakes beyond what someone that age would be given.

This idea has the shape: a thing that grows — something small in the main character's care gets bigger, and what it needs grows with it. Keep the shape; the shape is a requirement, not a choice.

Generate a story idea that includes:
1. THE SETUP: who is there and what they want.
2. WHAT STANDS IN THE WAY.
3. THE TURN: something that changes what the reader expected.
4. THE PROMISE: one thing that happens in this book.
5. WHAT IT COSTS THEM TO FAIL.

The reader already chose the town and the season. Do not open with an address. The place is the scene the action happens in, named where the action is, never a sentence that states where and when.

The want, the obstacle and the cost are each a concrete thing the reader can name: one thing to reach, fetch, mend or be in time for, a stated force or condition against it, and a stated loss. Wanting to find out what something is, an unnamed something standing in the way, or more than they can see, are none of the three.

Stop there. Never write how it ends, and never write the middle: no naming the object, gate, figure or trick that decides the outcome, no test the characters will have to pass, and no pairing of a character's trait with the obstacle it will meet. Say who they are, not what each of them will do about it.

STORY LENGTH: MEDIUM (11-20 pages) - 8 sentences max per idea

The page count sets how much story gets written later, never how much of it is given away here. A long book gets the same short back-cover text as a short one.

## WHAT MAKES A PARENT BUY IT

The idea answers these:
- What does the child get to do here that they cannot do at home?
- What in it will they laugh at, or gasp at?
- What is frightening here in the way a child likes being frightened?
- Which sentence makes them ask for this book again tomorrow?

RULES:
- No adjectives allowed. Do not describe things as "magical", "brave", "beautiful", "exciting", etc.
- Four to six sentences, whatever the page count, and at most one sentence per slot. A longer text turns into a plot summary.
- One sentence is the turn: something changes what the reader expected. The thing acts back, the wrong person is believed, the helper turns out to need help. It stands between the obstacle and the event, and it names neither the middle nor the ending.
- One sentence is an event this book contains, written in the story's voice as a thing that happens and can be pictured. It never addresses the reader and never names the reader, the book, the page or the picture. Never whether they manage it, and never what decides it. It stands after the obstacle.
- No sentence runs past about 30 words. A sentence that needs a dash to hold two clauses together is two sentences.
- The last sentence states what failing costs, and the cost is something of theirs. Nothing comes after it.
- [FINAL] holds the idea text only: no notes, no headings, no second version, no commentary.
- Nothing in the story or its pictures is dangerous enough that it could lead to death — for anyone. Frightening is the right level. No child is left alone at a height or on an edge, and no cost ends on a child never coming home. A historical event keeps the danger it really had: tell it at a child's level, never remove it.
- Be specific about locations and time periods.
- The outline should focus on the main characters
- All the characters must be mentioned
- A character is in the idea through what they want, what they are answerable for, or the part of the main character's want they hold: someone waiting for them, someone they fetch it for. That is presence.
- The youngest main character does something in the idea. An adult is in the idea only when the story needs them, and then they want something of their own.
- The want is the main character's own want, stated as theirs, and they are the one who sets out after it. An errand an adult handed them is not their want. For a main character aged two or under the want is something to reach, follow, touch, hold or get to, never an object to fetch back and never an arrangement to sort out.
- One thing in the idea is out of the ordinary and can be pointed at in a picture: a thing, a creature, a place or an event, named with a plain noun. It stands in the first or second sentence and belongs to the setup or to the obstacle, never to what decides the outcome. It is named and never explained: not what it does, not what it opens, not who it obeys, not why it is as it is.
- The want is one a child would have for themselves: something to reach, to keep, to get into, to be first at, to give to someone, or to be allowed. A submission, a measurement, a permit, a set of numbers, or a repair an adult is paid to do is not one.
- Follow the SCENE COMPLEXITY guide above - match story complexity to the number of scenes

EXAMPLES of good story ideas:

Example 1: "A stone in the wall of a ruin sits loose, and behind it is a way into somewhere that is on no map. A child wants the little carved animal their grandmother lost in there when she was small. Whoever keeps that gap says the animal belongs to him now. Then he says the grandmother's name, and he says it as though he has been waiting for her. The child squeezes through the wall with the evening bell already ringing at home. If the last bell goes first, the animal stays his, and the grandmother has only the story of it."

Example 2: "A bone as long as an arm lies half out of the gravel at the foot of a quarry. A child wants to carry it up to their grandfather, who is the only one who will know what animal it came from. An older brother says it is a stick and walks on, and the gate at the top of the path is locked when the sun goes down. The gravel slides, and there is more of the animal under it than one child can carry. The child kneels in the gravel and digs with both hands while the light turns orange. If the gate closes first, the whole of it goes back under, and nobody ever hears what it was."

Example 3: "A goat is standing on the kitchen table eating the birthday cake. A child wants that cake out in the garden, where everyone is already singing. The goat is bigger than the child and will not be pushed. The singing stops, and the whole garden decides it was the child who let the goat in. The child stands in the doorway and holds out an apple in both hands. If the cake never comes out, it stays the child's fault for as long as anyone remembers that birthday."

Output all three stages:

[REVIEW]
List exactly 5 improvements, even if the draft seems good. Never say "no issues" - always find ways to make it better.

A name with none of that is not in the story yet. For each adult, quote what they want of their own; an adult the story does not need comes out of [FINAL].
5. **Complexity**: Does it match the scene count guide? Too simple or too complex?

Replace that place in [FINAL]. Then quote any words that leave a child alone at a height or on an edge, and any words in the cost sentence that end on a child not coming home or not returning; replace the place, and replace that cost with a loss the child can bear. changed. Every one of those beats is on the page, in that order.

**A real low point is required.** Before the end there is a page where the plan has failed, the thing
is lost, or the friend is gone, and it looks like it will stay that way. Do not soften it into a
small setback and do not skip past it in a line.

**The hero's own idea turns it.** What saves the day comes out of the main character — something they
noticed earlier, a strength of theirs, a thing they were told and remembered. Never luck, never a
grown-up arriving to fix it, never a power handed over at the last moment.

**It resolves.** The turn comes before the last page and they come home changed. Never a story that
stops on the problem.

**A real antagonist is allowed.** Someone who wants something opposed to what the main character
wants, with a reason of their own. A twist, a sidekick who earns their place, and a setup on an early
page that pays off at the end all belong here.

**Competence.** The main character does things: decides, tries, fails, adapts. They are never carried
through their own story.

**The stake is the main character's own.** What is wanted and what is at risk belong to their own
life — never a piece of work set for them, an assignment, a submission, a competition entry, or a
place to be won in a selection. What stands in the way is something they can reach out and touch, or
someone who wants the opposite, never a procedure, a schedule or a system to be satisfied. What is at
risk is a person or a creature they care about, never a promise made to themselves, a recording or a
machine's state. The thing out of the ordinary is one they hold or touch, never one they operate.

nothing cruel, nobody the reader likes is really harmed.

**Ending.** They come back to where they started and it reads differently, because they are different.

**The age owns the props and the subject.** What the main character wants, what stands in the way, and the objects the story turns on belong to the world of someone that age — what they handle themselves, where they go on their own, what counts as a loss to them. Example 1: "A stone in the wall of a ruin sits loose, and behind it is a way into somewhere that is on no map. A child wants the little carved animal their grandmother lost in there when she was small. Whoever keeps that gap says the animal belongs to him now. Then he says the grandmother's name, and he says it as though he has been waiting for her. The child squeezes through the wall with the evening bell already ringing at home. If the last bell goes first, the animal stays his, and the grandmother has only the story of it."

Example 2: "A bone as long as an arm lies half out of the gravel at the foot of a quarry. A child wants to carry it up to their grandfather, who is the only one who will know what animal it came from. An older brother says it is a stick and walks on, and the gate at the top of the path is locked when the sun goes down. The gravel slides, and there is more of the animal under it than one child can carry. The child kneels in the gravel and digs with both hands while the light turns orange. If the gate closes first, the whole of it goes back under, and nobody ever hears what it was."

Example 3: "A goat is standing on the kitchen table eating the birthday cake. A child wants that cake out in the garden, where everyone is already singing. The goat is bigger than the child and will not be pushed. The singing stops, and the whole garden decides it was the child who let the goat in. The child stands in the doorway and holds out an apple in both hands. If the cake never comes out, it stays the child's fault for as long as anyone remembers that birthday."

**A real low point is required.** Before the end there is a page where the plan has failed, the thing

small setback and do not skip past it in a line.

Wanting to find out what something is, an unnamed something standing in the way, or more than they can see, are none of the three.

Never write how it ends, and never write the middle: no naming the object, gate, figure or trick that decides the outcome, no test the characters will have to pass, and no pairing of a character's trait with the obstacle it will meet. Say who they are, not what each of them will do about it.

STORY LENGTH: MEDIUM (11-20 pages) - 8 sentences max per idea

The page count sets how much story gets written later, never how much of it is given away here. A long book gets the same short back-cover text as a short one.

## WHAT MAKES A PARENT BUY IT

The idea answers these:
- What does the child get to do here that they cannot do at home?
- What in it will they laugh at, or gasp at?
- What is frightening here in the way a child likes being frightened?
- Which sentence makes them ask for this book again tomorrow?

RULES:
- No adjectives allowed. Do not describe things as "magical", "brave", "beautiful", "exciting", etc.
- Four to six sentences, whatever the page count, and at most one sentence per slot. A longer text turns into a plot summary.
- One sentence is the turn: something changes what the reader expected. The thing acts back, the wrong person is believed, the helper turns out to need help. It stands between the obstacle and the event, and it names neither the middle nor the ending.
- One sentence is an event this book contains, written in the story's voice as a thing that happens and can be pictured. It never addresses the reader and never names the reader, the book, the page or the picture. Never whether they manage it, and never what decides it. It stands after the obstacle.
- No sentence runs past about 30 words. A sentence that needs a dash to hold two clauses together is two sentences.
- The last sentence states what failing costs, and the cost is something of theirs. Nothing comes after it.
- [FINAL] holds the idea text only: no notes, no headings, no second version, no commentary.
- Nothing in the story or its pictures is dangerous enough that it could lead to death — for anyone. Frightening is the right level. No child is left alone at a height or on an edge, and no cost ends on a child never coming home. A historical event keeps the danger it really had: tell it at a child's level, never remove it.
- Be specific about locations and time periods.
- The outline should focus on the main characters
- All the characters must be mentioned
- A character is in the idea through what they want, what they are answerable for, or the part of the main character's want they hold: someone waiting for them, someone they fetch it for. That is presence.
- The youngest main character does something in the idea. An adult is in the idea only when the story needs them, and then they want something of their own.
- The want is the main character's own want, stated as theirs, and they are the one who sets out after it. An errand an adult handed them is not their want. For a main character aged two or under the want is something to reach, follow, touch, hold or get to, never an object to fetch back and never an arrangement to sort out.
- One thing in the idea is out of the ordinary and can be pointed at in a picture: a thing, a creature, a place or an event, named with a plain noun. It stands in the first or second sentence and belongs to the setup or to the obstacle, never to what decides the outcome. It is named and never explained: not what it does, not what it opens, not who it obeys, not why it is as it is.
- The want is one a child would have for themselves: something to reach, to keep, to get into, to be first at, to give to someone, or to be allowed. A submission, a measurement, a permit, a set of numbers, or a repair an adult is paid to do is not one.
- Follow the SCENE COMPLEXITY guide above - match story complexity to the number of scenes

EXAMPLES of good story ideas:

Example 1: "A stone in the wall of a ruin sits loose, and behind it is a way into somewhere that is on no map. A child wants the little carved animal their grandmother lost in there when she was small. Whoever keeps that gap says the animal belongs to him now. Then he says the grandmother's name, and he says it as though he has been waiting for her. The child squeezes through the wall with the evening bell already ringing at home. If the last bell goes first, the animal stays his, and the grandmother has only the story of it."

Example 2: "A bone as long as an arm lies half out of the gravel at the foot of a quarry. A child wants to carry it up to their grandfather, who is the only one who will know what animal it came from. An older brother says it is a stick and walks on, and the gate at the top of the path is locked when the sun goes down. The gravel slides, and there is more of the animal under it than one child can carry. The child kneels in the gravel and digs with both hands while the light turns orange. If the gate closes first, the whole of it goes back under, and nobody ever hears what it was."

Example 3: "A goat is standing on the kitchen table eating the birthday cake. A child wants that cake out in the garden, where everyone is already singing. The goat is bigger than the child and will not be pushed. The singing stops, and the whole garden decides it was the child who let the goat in. The child stands in the doorway and holds out an apple in both hands. If the cake never comes out, it stays the child's fault for as long as anyone remembers that birthday."

---

## GENERATION PROCESS:

Output all three stages:

[DRAFT]
Create your initial story outline following all guidelines above.

[REVIEW]
List exactly 5 improvements, even if the draft seems good. Never say "no issues" - always find ways to make it better.

FIRST CHECK - LANGUAGE: Is the entire draft written in the correct language as specified at the top? If you wrote in English but the language should be German/French/etc, this is an error that must be fixed in [FINAL].

Check and critique:
1. **Language**: Is the entire output in the correct language (not just terminology)? If wrong language, mark as an error.
2. **Formatting**:
   - No **bold** or *italic* (no asterisks)?
   - Plain paragraphs only (no headers, bullets, or lists)?
   - No adjectives (magical, brave, beautiful, exciting)?
   - Within sentence limits for the story length?
   - No sentence past about 30 words, and no dash holding two clauses together in one sentence?
3. **Logic & Consistency**:
   - Do events follow logically from each other?
   - Any plot holes or unexplained jumps?
   - Is the timeline coherent?
4. **Characters**: for each name, quote the words that put them in the idea: what they want, what they are answerable for, or the part of the main character's want they hold. A name with none of that is not in the story yet. For each adult, quote what they want of their own; an adult the story does not need comes out of [FINAL].
5. **Complexity**: Does it match the scene count guide? Too simple or too complex?
6. **Back cover, not synopsis**: number the sentences of [FINAL]. Label each one "setup", "hook", "turn", "promise", "event", "rule" or "cost". A "turn" is the sentence where something changes what the reader expected. A "promise" names an event the book contains, in the story's voice, and does not say whether they manage it. A "rule" is any sentence that says what only happens if, what opens only when, what resets, or what someone will not do — the condition a reader would use to work out the ending. Only "event" and "rule" are cut: every sentence marked "event" other than the last, and every sentence marked "rule". Setup, hook, turn, promise and cost are kept. The sentence marked "cost" names something of theirs that is lost. List every cut sentence, not one of them.
7. **Peril**: name the youngest character and their age, then quote the words that put them at a height, in deep or rising water, in the dark underground, or in a vehicle with a supply running out. Replace that place in [FINAL]. Then quote any words that leave a child alone at a height or on an edge, and any words in the cost sentence that end on a child not coming home or not returning; replace the place, and replace that cost with a loss the child can bear. A historical event keeps the danger it really had: tell it at a child's level, never remove it.
8. **Topic**: quote the words where the topic is what stands in the way. If the idea reads the same with the topic removed, rewrite it.
9. **Hook**: quote the noun that names the one thing out of the ordinary, and say which sentence it stands in. If there is nothing to quote, add one to [FINAL]. If the quoted thing is what decides the outcome, replace it with one that belongs to the setup or to the obstacle. Then quote any words that say what it does, what it opens, who it obeys, or why it is as it is, and cut them.
10. **The child acts**: quote the words where the main character wants, and the words where they set out after it. If the want is an adult's errand, or the words show them carried, brought or minded, rewrite both in [FINAL]. For a main character aged two or under the quoted want is something to reach, follow, touch, hold or get to. Say in one word what the child gets out of it. If the want is a submission, a measurement, a permit, a set of numbers or a repair, replace it with one a child would have.
11. **Promise**: quote the sentence that names an event the book contains. If there is nothing to quote, add one to [FINAL]. If it says whether they manage it, or what decides it, rewrite it. Then quote any words that address the reader or name the reader, the book, the page or the picture, and cut them.
12. **Turn**: quote the sentence where something changes what the reader expected. If there is nothing to quote, add one to [FINAL]. If it says how the story goes on from there, or how it ends, rewrite it.
13. **Shape**: name the shape you were given and quote the words in [FINAL] that carry it. If it is not there, rewrite [FINAL] to the shape.
14. **Opening**: quote the first sentence. If it states where and when rather than showing the hook or the main character, rewrite it.
15. **Length**: count the sentences of [FINAL] and the words of the longest one. Past six sentences, or past 30 words, split or cut before [FINAL].
16. **Would a parent buy it**: answer each of these with a quote from [FINAL].
- What does the child get to do here that they cannot do at home?
- What in it will they laugh at, or gasp at?
- What is frightening here in the way a child likes being frightened?
- Which sentence makes them ask for this book again tomorrow?
A question with no quote to answer it means that part of [FINAL] gets rewritten until there is one. This is the last check, and it outranks the others: an idea that survives every check above and answers none of these is not worth printing.

List your 5 improvements (be specific):

[FINAL]
The corrected, final version of the story idea.

[DRAFT]

Dans la cuisine du château de Pierrefort, Cuisinière Margot prépare chaque matin un repas pour soixante personnes sans que personne ne la remercie. Chloé, qui dort sur une paillasse près du feu, est la seule à lui dire bonjour. Quand le chevalier principal accuse Margot d'avoir volé le sceau du seigneur, tout le monde le croit. Théo, le frère de Chloé, est du mauvais côté du pont-levis qui vient de se lever. Maman Élodie, qui garde la porte du donjon, refuse de laisser entrer Chloé pour parler au seigneur. Chloé traverse la cuisine vide, prend le message que Margot lui a glissé dans la main, et part le porter au seigneur elle-même. Si le seigneur signe l'ordre avant que Chloé arrive, Margot quitte le château ce soir, et il n'y a plus personne pour allumer le feu demain matin.

[REVIEW]

FIRST CHECK — LANGUAGE: Le brouillon est en français. La typographie suisse doit encore être appliquée (guillemets, pas d'espace avant la ponctuation). Aucune ligne de dialogue ici, donc le problème est moindre, mais le registre et le vocabulaire suisse doivent être vérifiés.

1. Langue: Le texte est en français. Le vocabulaire suisse est absent: «soixante» devrait rester (c'est un nombre normal), mais il faut vérifier «dîner/souper» etc. Ici aucun repas n'est nommé mais «cuisine» est correct. Registre globalement correct. Pas d'erreur majeure de langue, mais «paillasse» est correct et suisse. Vérifier qu'aucun anglicisme ne s'est glissé.

2. Formatage: Pas de gras, pas d'italique. Pas de listes. Pas d'adjectifs? «principal» qualifie un nom commun — à vérifier: «le chevalier principal» — c'est plutôt un titre. «vide» dans «cuisine vide» — c'est un adjectif. À supprimer. Pas de phrase dépassant 30 mots? La dernière phrase est longue: «Si le seigneur signe l'ordre avant que Chloé arrive, Margot quitte le château ce soir, et il n'y a plus personne pour allumer le feu demain matin.» — à compter: 32 mots environ. À couper.

3. Logique: Théo est de l'autre côté du pont-levis — mais il n'a pas encore eu de raison d'être là. Et sa présence n'est pas exploitée dans la suite. Le pont-levis monte sans raison narrative. Maman Élodie garde la porte du donjon — pourquoi? Elle n'a pas de vouloir propre clairement identifié.

4. Personnages: Chloé — «la seule à lui dire bonjour» / «prend le message» / «part le porter». Présente. Théo — «est du mauvais côté du pont-levis» — ce qu'il est answerable for: rien. Aucun vouloir propre. À corriger. Maman Élodie — «refuse de laisser entrer Chloé» — elle a un vouloir propre (garder la porte), mais il est mince. La règle: un adulte n'est dans l'idée que si l'histoire en a besoin, et il veut quelque chose de son propre chef.

5. Complexité: L'idée a une intrigue principale (sauver Margot) et un élément secondaire (Théo séparé, Maman Élodie en obstacle). Convient pour un récit de 12 scènes. Correct.

6. Analyse phrase par phrase:
— «Dans la cuisine du château de Pierrefort, Cuisinière Margot prépare chaque matin un repas pour soixante personnes sans que personne ne la remercie.» → SETUP
— «Chloé, qui dort sur une paillasse près du feu, est la seule à lui dire bonjour.» → SETUP
— «Quand le chevalier principal accuse Margot d'avoir volé le sceau du seigneur, tout le monde le croit.» → TURN
— «Théo, le frère de Chloé, est du mauvais côté du pont-levis qui vient de se lever.» → HOOK (chose hors de l'ordinaire: le pont-levis)
— «Maman Élodie, qui garde la porte du donjon, refuse de laisser entrer Chloé pour parler au seigneur.» → OBSTACLE
— «Chloé traverse la cuisine vide, prend le message que Margot lui a glissé dans la main, et part le porter au seigneur elle-même.» → PROMISE (événement du livre)
— «Si le seigneur signe l'ordre avant que Chloé arrive, Margot quitte le château ce soir, et il n'y a plus personne pour allumer le feu demain matin.» → COST

Phrases marquées EVENT: aucune à couper. Phrases marquées RULE: aucune. Phrase PROMISE: «Chloé traverse la cuisine vide» — l'adjectif «vide» est à supprimer. Pas de phrase marquée EVENT à couper. Le test de back cover est satisfait dans l'ensemble mais deux phrases de setup peuvent être fusionnées.

CUT (check 6): rien à couper selon les règles, mais «vide» et «principal» (adjectifs) sont à retirer.

7. Péril: Chloé a 6 ans. Elle ne se retrouve pas en hauteur, dans l'eau, dans le noir souterrain ou dans un véhicule. Aucun péril physique extrême. Le coût final («Margot quitte le château ce soir, et il n'y a plus personne pour allumer le feu demain matin») ne laisse pas un enfant sans rentrer chez lui. Correct.

8. Sujet (knights): Le chevalier est celui qui fait la fausse accusation. C'est le tournant narratif. L'idée ne se lit pas pareil sans lui. Correct.

9. Hook: Le pont-levis qui se lève avec Théo du mauvais côté est la chose hors de l'ordinaire. Mais il est dans la quatrième phrase — à déplacer plus tôt. Et il ne dit pas ce qu'il fait ni pourquoi. Correct sur ce point.

10. L'enfant agit: Chloé «prend le message» et «part le porter» — elle agit de son propre chef. Son vouloir: sauver Margot. Ce n'est pas une course confiée par un adulte — Margot lui glisse le message mais c'est Chloé qui décide de partir. Le vouloir est le sien. Correct. Ce qu'elle en retire: justice.

11. Promise: «Chloé traverse la cuisine [vide], prend le message que Margot lui a glissé dans la main, et part le porter au seigneur elle-même.» — c'est un événement concret du livre, dit dans la voix du récit. Ne dit pas si elle réussit. Correct, mais l'adjectif «vide» doit disparaître.

12. Turn: «Quand le chevalier principal accuse Margot d'avoir volé le sceau du seigneur, tout le monde le croit.» — change ce qu'on attendait. Correct. Mais «principal» est un adjectif à supprimer. Remplacer par «le chevalier en chef» ou simplement «le chevalier».

13. Shape: Message à porter — Chloé doit porter un message au seigneur avant qu'il signe l'ordre. La forme est présente. Correct.

14. Opening: «Dans la cuisine du château de Pierrefort, Cuisinière Margot prépare chaque matin un repas pour soixante personnes sans que personne ne la remercie.» — cette phrase déclare un lieu et une habitude plutôt que de plonger dans l'action ou le personnage principal. Elle ne montre pas Chloé. À réécrire pour placer Chloé au centre dès le début.

15. Longueur: 7 phrases — une de trop. Limite: 6 max. La dernière phrase dépasse 30 mots. Une des deux phrases de setup peut être supprimée ou fusionnée.

16. Parent achèterait-il?
— Ce que l'enfant peut faire ici qu'il ne peut pas faire à la maison: porter un message dans un château, franchir des obstacles pour sauver quelqu'un. Oui, implicite.
— Ce qui fait rire ou souffler: le pont-levis qui monte au mauvais moment — ça, ça peut. Mais ce n'est pas assez fort.
— Ce qui fait peur à la façon dont un enfant aime avoir peur: Margot chassée du château ce soir — c'est doux. À renforcer légèrement.
— La phrase qu'on veut relire: la dernière («il n'y a plus personne pour allumer le feu demain matin») a du potentiel, mais la formule est un peu ordinaire.

5 améliorations:

1. Supprimer les adjectifs «vide» et «principal» et réduire à 6 phrases maximum en fusionnant les deux phrases de setup.
2. Réécrire l'ouverture pour placer Chloé au centre dès la première phrase plutôt que de commencer par Margot et le château.
3. Donner à Théo un vouloir propre ou une responsabilité concrète dans l'idée — il ne peut pas être présent uniquement comme obstacle géographique.
4. Donner à Maman Élodie un vouloir propre plus précis pour justifier sa présence narrative.
5. Raccourcir la phrase du coût sous 30 mots et la rendre plus frappante pour l'œil d'un parent.

CUT: rien à couper selon le check 6 (aucune phrase EVENT ni RULE). «vide» et «principal» sont supprimés comme adjectifs.

[FINAL]

Chloé dort sur une paillasse près du feu de la cuisine du château, et chaque matin c'est Cuisinière Margot qui allume ce feu pour les soixante bouches du château — sans que personne ne la remercie. Quand le chevalier en armure accuse Margot d'avoir volé le sceau du seigneur, tout le monde le croit, et personne ne demande à Margot ce qu'elle en sait. Le pont-levis se lève au même moment, et Théo, le frère de Chloé, se retrouve de l'autre côté sans pouvoir revenir. Maman Élodie garde la porte du donjon et veut que l'ordre du seigneur soit appliqué: personne ne passe. Chloé prend le message que Margot lui a glissé dans la main et part le porter au seigneur elle-même, à travers les couloirs de pierre et les gardes du matin. Si le seigneur signe avant qu'elle arrive, Margot quitte le château ce soir, et le feu ne sera plus allumé pour personne.

The story should help children understand and cope with this topic.

**TOPIC GUIDE for "managing-emotions":**
**What the book is.** A big feeling — anger, frustration, sadness — from the moment
it arrives to the moment it passes.

**What happens.** The feeling shows in the body first: tight fists, a hot face,
tears, the wanting to shout. It gets named out loud, which is where it starts to
loosen. Then something is done with it — breathing, counting, a pillow squeezed,
a quiet corner gone to. Afterwards, once it has passed, what happened is talked
through and the actual problem gets dealt with.

**Where the line is.** Hitting, kicking and breaking things stay out, however big
the feeling is. That holds throughout.

**Adults too.** Somebody grown up has a big feeling in this book and handles it in
front of the child.

**What it is not.** Not a feeling called bad, and not a child who is calm by
choosing to be.

**Ending.** Through it, sitting with somebody, the thing sorted out.

**ADVENTURE SETTING GUIDE for "dragon":**
COSTUME: not needed - use standard, summer or winter avatar

Who lives here (pick one):

- An old dragon who is losing her fire and pretends otherwise
- A dragon the size of a cat who cannot fly yet and is hiding it

- A young dragon who has lost the one thing from the hoard it cared about

- A dragon who will carry someone once, today, and never again
- A dragon who is afraid of something much smaller than itself

What turns (pick one):

- The promise made to a dragon is easier to give than to keep
- The fire will not light, and it has never failed before
- The flight was for one, and there are two who need it
- The hoard is counted and one thing is missing that nobody may mention
- The cave mouth opens when the mist lifts, and the mist is coming back
- The elder speaks so slowly that the answer comes too late to use
- What the dragon wants is not what everyone assumed dragons want
- Being trusted by one means being distrusted by the rest

Story entry points (pick one or combine):
- Full dragon-world adventure from the start
- A dragon egg found somewhere very ordinary

- A picture book whose dragon climbs off the page

Story guidance:
- Set in mountain eyries, valleys of mist, volcanic ridges, cloud-high skies, hoards in deep caves

- Give each dragon a scale and a manner - a shoulder-sized small one, a cart-sized young one, a mountain-sized elder who speaks slowly

## CHALLENGE IDEAS (a sample from a catalogue of classic trials)
When the story needs an obstacle, prefer one of these — or one in their spirit — over the usual stream, boulder, locked gate, refusing guard or storm. Pick what fits the characters and the world; vary the kind.

# HERO'S JOURNEY (age 8)

The child this book is for is eight. Write for that child.

**The full shape, at full size.** Ordinary world, then a call that pulls the main character out of it,
then challenges that get harder, then a moment where all seems lost, then the turn, then home —
changed. Every one of those beats is on the page, in that order.

**A real low point is required.** Before the end there is a page where the plan has failed, the thing
is lost, or the friend is gone, and it looks like it will stay that way. Do not soften it into a
small setback and do not skip past it in a line.

**The hero's own idea turns it.** What saves the day comes out of the main character — something they
noticed earlier, a strength of theirs, a thing they were told and remembered. Never luck, never a
grown-up arriving to fix it, never a power handed over at the last moment.

**It resolves.** The turn comes before the last page and they come home changed. Never a story that
stops on the problem.

**A real antagonist is allowed.** Someone who wants something opposed to what the main character
wants, with a reason of their own. A twist, a sidekick who earns their place, and a setup on an early
page that pays off at the end all belong here.

**Competence.** The main character does things: decides, tries, fails, adapts. They are never carried
through their own story.

**The stake is the main character's own.** What is wanted and what is at risk belong to their own
life — never a piece of work set for them, an assignment, a submission, a competition entry, or a
place to be won in a selection. What stands in the way is something they can reach out and touch, or
someone who wants the opposite, never a procedure, a schedule or a system to be satisfied. What is at
risk is a person or a creature they care about, never a promise made to themselves, a recording or a
machine's state. The thing out of the ordinary is one they hold or touch, never one they operate.

**Humour and mild peril.** A chase, a close call, a night out in the cold are fine. Nothing gory,
nothing cruel, nobody the reader likes is really harmed.

**Ending.** They come back to where they started and it reads differently, because they are different.

**The age owns the props and the subject.** What the main character wants, what stands in the way, and the objects the story turns on belong to the world of someone that age — what they handle themselves, where they go on their own, what counts as a loss to them. Never a want, a comfort or a plaything the reader has outgrown, and never stakes beyond what someone that age would be given.

This idea has the shape: a swap or a mix-up — two things, or two people, are taken for each other, and everyone acts on the wrong one. Keep the shape; the shape is a requirement, not a choice.

Generate a story idea that includes:
1. THE SETUP: who is there and what they want.
2. WHAT STANDS IN THE WAY.
3. THE TURN: something that changes what the reader expected.
4. THE PROMISE: one thing that happens in this book.
5. WHAT IT COSTS THEM TO FAIL.

The reader already chose the town and the season. Do not open with an address. The place is the scene the action happens in, named where the action is, never a sentence that states where and when.

The want, the obstacle and the cost are each a concrete thing the reader can name: one thing to reach, fetch, mend or be in time for, a stated force or condition against it, and a stated loss. Wanting to find out what something is, an unnamed something standing in the way, or more than they can see, are none of the three.

Stop there. Never write how it ends, and never write the middle: no naming the object, gate, figure or trick that decides the outcome, no test the characters will have to pass, and no pairing of a character's trait with the obstacle it will meet. Say who they are, not what each of them will do about it.

STORY LENGTH: MEDIUM (11-20 pages) - 8 sentences max per idea

The page count sets how much story gets written later, never how much of it is given away here. A long book gets the same short back-cover text as a short one.

## WHAT MAKES A PARENT BUY IT

The idea answers these:
- What does the child get to do here that they cannot do at home?
- What in it will they laugh at, or gasp at?
- What is frightening here in the way a child likes being frightened?
- Which sentence makes them ask for this book again tomorrow?

RULES:
- No adjectives allowed. Do not describe things as "magical", "brave", "beautiful", "exciting", etc.
- Four to six sentences, whatever the page count, and at most one sentence per slot. A longer text turns into a plot summary.
- One sentence is the turn: something changes what the reader expected. The thing acts back, the wrong person is believed, the helper turns out to need help. It stands between the obstacle and the event, and it names neither the middle nor the ending.
- One sentence is an event this book contains, written in the story's voice as a thing that happens and can be pictured. It never addresses the reader and never names the reader, the book, the page or the picture. Never whether they manage it, and never what decides it. It stands after the obstacle.
- No sentence runs past about 30 words. A sentence that needs a dash to hold two clauses together is two sentences.
- The last sentence states what failing costs, and the cost is something of theirs. Nothing comes after it.
- [FINAL] holds the idea text only: no notes, no headings, no second version, no commentary.
- Nothing in the story or its pictures is dangerous enough that it could lead to death — for anyone. Frightening is the right level. No child is left alone at a height or on an edge, and no cost ends on a child never coming home. A historical event keeps the danger it really had: tell it at a child's level, never remove it.
- Be specific about locations and time periods.
- The outline should focus on the main characters
- All the characters must be mentioned
- A character is in the idea through what they want, what they are answerable for, or the part of the main character's want they hold: someone waiting for them, someone they fetch it for. That is presence.
- The youngest main character does something in the idea. An adult is in the idea only when the story needs them, and then they want something of their own.
- The want is the main character's own want, stated as theirs, and they are the one who sets out after it. An errand an adult handed them is not their want. For a main character aged two or under the want is something to reach, follow, touch, hold or get to, never an object to fetch back and never an arrangement to sort out.
- One thing in the idea is out of the ordinary and can be pointed at in a picture: a thing, a creature, a place or an event, named with a plain noun. It stands in the first or second sentence and belongs to the setup or to the obstacle, never to what decides the outcome. It is named and never explained: not what it does, not what it opens, not who it obeys, not why it is as it is.
- The want is one a child would have for themselves: something to reach, to keep, to get into, to be first at, to give to someone, or to be allowed. A submission, a measurement, a permit, a set of numbers, or a repair an adult is paid to do is not one.
- Follow the SCENE COMPLEXITY guide above - match story complexity to the number of scenes

EXAMPLES of good story ideas:

Example 1: "A stone in the wall of a ruin sits loose, and behind it is a way into somewhere that is on no map. A child wants the little carved animal their grandmother lost in there when she was small. Whoever keeps that gap says the animal belongs to him now. Then he says the grandmother's name, and he says it as though he has been waiting for her. The child squeezes through the wall with the evening bell already ringing at home. If the last bell goes first, the animal stays his, and the grandmother has only the story of it."

Example 2: "A bone as long as an arm lies half out of the gravel at the foot of a quarry. A child wants to carry it up to their grandfather, who is the only one who will know what animal it came from. An older brother says it is a stick and walks on, and the gate at the top of the path is locked when the sun goes down. The gravel slides, and there is more of the animal under it than one child can carry. The child kneels in the gravel and digs with both hands while the light turns orange. If the gate closes first, the whole of it goes back under, and nobody ever hears what it was."

Example 3: "A goat is standing on the kitchen table eating the birthday cake. A child wants that cake out in the garden, where everyone is already singing. The goat is bigger than the child and will not be pushed. The singing stops, and the whole garden decides it was the child who let the goat in. The child stands in the doorway and holds out an apple in both hands. If the cake never comes out, it stays the child's fault for as long as anyone remembers that birthday."

13. Form (Shape): Die vorgegebene Form ist «Verwechslung / Vertauschung». Das ist vorhanden: Beide Kinder wurden derselben Geschichte zugeführt und glauben, der Eine zu sein — eine Vertauschung der Zuschreibung. Form ist vorhanden.

14. Eröffnung: «In den Felsen des Teufelskellers, am Osthang oberhalb von Baden, hat sich etwas Grosses eingenistet.» — Das ist konkret, zeigt den Ort durch die Handlung (etwas nistet sich ein), nennt kein «Es war einmal» und keinen Kalender. Gut.

15. Länge: 6 Sätze. Längster Satz prüfen: «Mila will dasselbe, weil ihr dieselbe Geschichte erzählt wurde und sie dieselbe Schlussfolgerung gezogen hat.» — ca. 19 Wörter. Passt. Satz 6: «Verras trägt nur einmal, heute, und danach nie wieder; wer zurückbleibt, bleibt zurück, während der andere in die Wolken steigt.» — ca. 23 Wörter, aber der Strichpunkt hält zwei Teilsätze zusammen. Das entspricht einem Gedankenstrich, der zwei Hauptsätze verbindet. Muss aufgeteilt werden.

16. Würde ein Elternteil es kaufen?
— Was kann das Kind hier tun, was es zu Hause nicht kann? Einen uralten Drachen finden. Quote: «etwas Grosses eingenistet» / «Verras». Vorhanden.
— Worüber wird es lachen oder staunen? Noch unklar — kein Moment des Staunens oder leichten Humors. Fehlt.
— Was ist hier erschreckend, so wie ein Kind es gerne erschreckend hat? «hat Platz für genau einen» — das ist Spannung, aber der Schauer fehlt noch.
— Welcher Satz lässt es das Buch morgen wieder verlangen? Noch keiner.

VERBESSERUNGEN:
1. Das Thema «Gefühle bewältigen» muss sichtbar ins Hindernis eingebaut werden — der Konflikt zwischen Jonas und Mila entsteht, weil die Gefühle beider (Ärger, das Recht zu haben, Enttäuschung) sich in den Weg stellen.
2. Den Promise-Satz ergänzen: ein Ereignis, das im Buch stattfindet, in der Stimme der Geschichte.
3. Satz 6 aufteilen, weil Strichpunkt zwei Hauptsätze bindet.
4. «bernsteinfarben» streichen (verbotenes Adjektiv).
5. Einen Moment des Staunens oder leichten Humors einbauen, der Eltern und Kinder anspricht.

CUT: Satz 4 («Verras ist so alt wie der Berg, seine Schuppen leuchten bernsteinfarben im Oktoberlicht, und er hat Platz für genau einen.») wird als Ganzes überarbeitet — «bernsteinfarben» muss raus; «hat Platz für genau einen» ist eine Regel-Aussage, aber da kein «Rule»-Label sie ausschliesst (es ist die Kernspannung), bleibt die Information, aber die Formulierung wird vereinfacht. Nichts vollständig zu kürzen ausser der Adjektiv-Überarbeitung.

[FINAL]

In den Felsen des Teufelskellers, am Osthang oberhalb von Baden, hat sich ein Drache eingenistet, der vor Jahrzehnten einer Familie versprochen hat, einmal jemanden zu tragen. Jonas will dorthin, weil er überzeugt ist, dieser Jemand zu sein. Mila will dasselbe, und die Geschichte, die ihr erzählt wurde, klingt genauso wie die seine. Dann spricht Verras einen Namen aus — und beide Kinder halten den Atem an, denn beide haben diesen Namen ihr Leben lang gehört. Auf dem Felsvorsprung vor der Höhle streiten sich die zwei, und das Einzige, was Verras sagt, ist, dass er heute trägt — ein einziges Mal, und nie wieder. Wer zurückbleibt, bleibt zurück.

Your academic background means you deeply understand narrative structure, character psychology, and the craft of storytelling. You believe that children deserve the same quality of writing as adults - with rich character development, internally consistent plots, and prose that flows naturally.

**NO QUESTIONS - JUST DO IT**

Produce the complete output immediately using only the information provided below. Make reasonable creative decisions if anything is unclear.

Your strengths:
- **Character development**: Every character has believable motivations and grows through the story
- **Internal logic**: Plot events follow naturally from what came before - no forced coincidences or illogical jumps

Your task:
Write what stands on the back of the book. It tells a reader who this is about, where they are, what they want and what is in the way — and stops there. It never reports how the story goes or how it ends.

STORY CATEGORY: Life Skills

STORY TOPIC: <user_input>managing-emotions</user_input>

CHARACTERS:

- Mila: 8 years old, female, main character

RELATIONSHIPS:

READING LEVEL: Standard (7-9 year olds)

- Main storyline PLUS one secondary element or subplot
- At least 2 interwoven themes or character developments
- 6-8 key events with meaningful progression

IMPORTANT: This is a LIFE SKILLS story about "managing-emotions".
The story should help children understand and cope with this topic.
Show the characters facing this challenge and learning to handle it.
What stands in the way is this skill being hard, met in one outside event — never a feeling on its own.

**TOPIC GUIDE for "managing-emotions":**
**What the book is.** A big feeling — anger, frustration, sadness — from the moment
it arrives to the moment it passes.

**What happens.** The feeling shows in the body first: tight fists, a hot face,
tears, the wanting to shout. It gets named out loud, which is where it starts to
loosen. Then something is done with it — breathing, counting, a pillow squeezed,
a quiet corner gone to. Afterwards, once it has passed, what happened is talked
through and the actual problem gets dealt with.

**Where the line is.** Hitting, kicking and breaking things stay out, however big
the feeling is. That holds throughout.

**Adults too.** Somebody grown up has a big feeling in this book and handles it in
front of the child.

**What it is not.** Not a feeling called bad, and not a child who is calm by
choosing to be.

**Ending.** Through it, sitting with somebody, the thing sorted out.

**ADVENTURE SETTING GUIDE for "dragon":**
COSTUME: not needed - use standard, summer or winter avatar

Who lives here (pick one):
- An egg found somewhere very ordinary
- A hatchling who has decided who its family is
- An old dragon who is losing her fire and pretends otherwise
- A dragon the size of a cat who cannot fly yet and is hiding it
- A dragon who made a promise long ago and has come back to keep it
- A young dragon who has lost the one thing from the hoard it cared about
- A dragon who is not allowed to join the others and watches from a ledge
- Two hatchlings who have been swapped between nests
- A dragon who will carry someone once, today, and never again
- A dragon who is afraid of something much smaller than itself

What turns (pick one):
- The egg starts to move, and it is nowhere near a nest
- The one who was feared turns out to be the one who is frightened
- The promise made to a dragon is easier to give than to keep
- The fire will not light, and it has never failed before
- The flight was for one, and there are two who need it
- The hoard is counted and one thing is missing that nobody may mention
- The cave mouth opens when the mist lifts, and the mist is coming back
- The elder speaks so slowly that the answer comes too late to use
- What the dragon wants is not what everyone assumed dragons want
- Being trusted by one means being distrusted by the rest

Story entry points (pick one or combine):
- Full dragon-world adventure from the start
- A dragon egg found somewhere very ordinary
- A cave behind a waterfall that opens on another land
- Dream of flying above the clouds on a warm back
- A picture book whose dragon climbs off the page
- A kite that turns out to be alive
- A scale found on the path that is far too big
- Being chosen as a dragon's rider

Story guidance:
- Set in mountain eyries, valleys of mist, volcanic ridges, cloud-high skies, hoards in deep caves
- Dragons are characters, not monsters: they have names, moods, families, likes and worries
- Give each dragon a scale and a manner - a shoulder-sized small one, a cart-sized young one, a mountain-sized elder who speaks slowly
- Flight, warmth and smoke are the wonders; scorching, burnt villages and hunting are not
- Focus on trust between very different creatures, earning a friendship, keeping a promise, being small and brave
- Fire is shown as warmth, light, a cooked meal or a signal - never as harm
- Key props: dragon egg, single large scale, saddle and harness, a hot spring
- The idea is built on one centre and one turn, never on the props.

This idea starts from this centre and this turn. Centre: A hatchling who has decided who its family is. Turn: The elder speaks so slowly that the answer comes too late to use. Swap one only if it cannot fit the cast or the topic; keep the other.

## CHALLENGE IDEAS (a sample from a catalogue of classic trials)
When the story needs an obstacle, prefer one of these — or one in their spirit — over the usual stream, boulder, locked gate, refusing guard or storm. Pick what fits the characters and the world; vary the kind.

**SEASON**: It is Autumn. The season shows in the light, the weather, what is underfoot and what the cast wears — in an invented world too. It never decides what the story is about: any subject, any plot, any place can happen in autumn.

(3) Use Swiss vocabulary: "Bub" (not "Junge"), "Kappe" (not "Mütze"), "Rüebli" (not "Karotte"), "Velo" (not "Fahrrad"), "parkieren" (not "parken"), "grillieren" (not "grillen"), "Trottoir" (not "Bürgersteig"), "Lavabo" (not "Waschbecken"), "Natel" (not "Handy"), "Poulet" (not "Hähnchen"), "Glace" (not "Eis"), "Znüni/Zvieri" for snacks. NO space before !?:; CORRECT: "grösser", "süss", "das Velo", "das Rüebli", "parkieren", "das Poulet", «Wie geht es dir?» | WRONG: "größer", "süß", "das Fahrrad", "die Karotte", "parken", "das Hähnchen", « Wie geht es dir ? » (spaces inside guillemets), — Wie geht es dir? (em-dash for dialogue open). QUOTATION MARKS: never open one of a kind inside another of the same kind, and never leave one unclosed.**

Your entire output must be in the language specified above.
- All text in [DRAFT], [REVIEW], and [FINAL] sections must be in this language
